messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Error in analysis: post-stratified: ** Internal Error 102: Could not evaluate area under CDF. **
parts:
Sara

You can see from the warning messages that Distance is struggling to fit detection functions to your data.  I have a suspicion that the detection distance histograms do not look "well behaved".  This could be caused by a number of things.  My suspicion is that there are too few detections in one (several) of your size categories.  That is a problem that can easily occur with post-stratification; when not incorporating features of interest into the study design (via stratification) you are left to chance whether your strata groups are going to be adequately represented.

However, rather than requiring each strata to have sufficient detections to fit a detection function, consider using size as a (factor) covariate.  In this way you are using information from all size classes to fit the general shape of the function, with data from each strata used to estimate coefficients that alter the shape of the detection function.  You can continue to use size as a post-stratification criterion, this will permit estimation for each size class.  Is it important that you produce an estimate for each size class?

messages.author: 09607d3641d0afd1
messages.subject: Re: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Error in analysis: post-stratified: ** Internal Error 102: Could not evaluate area under CDF. **
parts:
Sara

You've been busy fitting models, but I think you've probably done more fitting than is necessary.  Post-stratification is used if you want to estimate density of categories of objects and those categories are not known to you at the time the study was designed.  Covariates are used if attributes of objects influence detectability and you wish to incorporate that information into your detection function modelling; most often you still achieve adequate estimates even if these covariates are not included in the modelling.

You indicate that there are large differences in estimates between the various models you have fitted.  Those differences must be taken in the context of the uncertainty in those estimates.  Looking at your model results table, and setting aside analyses 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18, density estimates from the other 14 models range between 5 and 9; but note all have confidence intervals between 3 and 12.  In that lights, I'd say there is not considerable variation in estimates between models.

However, you should use model selection tools and more judicious selection of models to fit to guide you to the best model for your data.  As you note, AIC is supposed to assist in model selection.  You are right to be concerned that most of your delta-AIC values are zero.  This is because when data are altered between models, AICs of those models are not comparable.  Note the column fourth from the left (with what appears to be a funnel at the top).  This is the model filter applied to the data for that analysis.  You will see you have applied 18 different filters to your 19 analyses.  The only analyses that used the same filter is analysis 4 and 5 (that is the reason you have a non-zero delta-AIC for analysis 5).  I'm not sure why you were changing your data filters for almost each analysis.  That should be something that changes very little, some initial investigation of truncation then no more alterations to the data filter among analyses.

The modelling decisions you make are driven by the objectives of your study.  If you have adequate fit of simple models and those inferences suit your objectives, then your analysis has reached its conclusion.

domingo, 25 de Agosto de 2019 às 15:53:17 UTC+1, Eric R escreveu:

Sara

You've been busy fitting models, but I think you've probably done more fitting than is necessary.  Post-stratification is used if you want to estimate density of categories of objects and those categories are not known to you at the time the study was designed.  Covariates are used if attributes of objects influence detectability and you wish to incorporate that information into your detection function modelling; most often you still achieve adequate estimates even if these covariates are not included in the modelling.

You indicate that there are large differences in estimates between the various models you have fitted.  Those differences must be taken in the context of the uncertainty in those estimates.  Looking at your model results table, and setting aside analyses 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18, density estimates from the other 14 models range between 5 and 9; but note all have confidence intervals between 3 and 12.  In that lights, I'd say there is not considerable variation in estimates between models.

However, you should use model selection tools and more judicious selection of models to fit to guide you to the best model for your data.  As you note, AIC is supposed to assist in model selection.  You are right to be concerned that most of your delta-AIC values are zero.  This is because when data are altered between models, AICs of those models are not comparable.  Note the column fourth from the left (with what appears to be a funnel at the top).  This is the model filter applied to the data for that analysis.  You will see you have applied 18 different filters to your 19 analyses.  The only analyses that used the same filter is analysis 4 and 5 (that is the reason you have a non-zero delta-AIC for analysis 5).  I'm not sure why you were changing your data filters for almost each analysis.  That should be something that changes very little, some initial investigation of truncation then no more alterations to the data filter among analyses.

The modelling decisions you make are driven by the objectives of your study.  If you have adequate fit of simple models and those inferences suit your objectives, then your analysis has reached its conclusion.

Let me clarify.  If you do not know the location of the types of objects for which you wish to stratify, then use post-stratification.

From the histograms of your data, it appears that you have only a 1 in 4 chance of seeing objects that are between 7 and 14m from the transect--roughly the same as objects 100m from the transect.  How is this possible?  If the objects seen at 100m are of large sizes, perhaps you might consider filtering your data into types (big and small) and fitting separate detection functions to each--and likely also using different truncation distances for each type.  Is that a plausible explanation for this pattern in your histograms?

The detection function shown in  the figures will result in extremely large estimates of density/abundance because the estimated probability of detection arising from a function of that shape is very small--implying a large proportion of objects are missed.  Let's continue to discuss off of the list, then you can provide your conclusions to the list when the situation is more clear.

You've been busy fitting models, but I think you've probably done more fitting than is necessary.  Post-stratification is used if you want to estimate density of categories of objects and those categories are not known to you at the time the study was designed.  Covariates are used if attributes of objects influence detectability and you wish to incorporate that information into your detection function modelling; most often you still achieve adequate estimates even if these covariates are not included in the modelling.

You indicate that there are large differences in estimates between the various models you have fitted.  Those differences must be taken in the context of the uncertainty in those estimates.  Looking at your model results table, and setting aside analyses 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18, density estimates from the other 14 models range between 5 and 9; but note all have confidence intervals between 3 and 12.  In that lights, I'd say there is not considerable variation in estimates between models.

However, you should use model selection tools and more judicious selection of models to fit to guide you to the best model for your data.  As you note, AIC is supposed to assist in model selection.  You are right to be concerned that most of your delta-AIC values are zero.  This is because when data are altered between models, AICs of those models are not comparable.  Note the column fourth from the left (with what appears to be a funnel at the top).  This is the model filter applied to the data for that analysis.  You will see you have applied 18 different filters to your 19 analyses.  The only analyses that used the same filter is analysis 4 and 5 (that is the reason you have a non-zero delta-AIC for analysis 5).  I'm not sure why you were changing your data filters for almost each analysis.  That should be something that changes very little, some initial investigation of truncation then no more alterations to the data filter among analyses.

The modelling decisions you make are driven by the objectives of your study.  If you have adequate fit of simple models and those inferences suit your objectives, then your analysis has reached its conclusion.
